subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 38-year-old woman has a painless anterior neck mass. She received radiation to the head and neck during childhood. Palpable cervical lymph nodes are present. Biopsy shows empty-appearing nuclei with central clearing, nuclear grooves, and concentric laminated calcifications.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Papillary carcinoma
Follicular carcinoma
Medullary carcinoma
Anaplastic carcinoma
Follicular adenoma

explanation_correct: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer. It is associated with childhood irradiation and with RET/PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations. Histology shows empty-appearing nuclei with central clearing (Orphan Annie eyes), nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies. It commonly metastasizes to cervical lymph nodes, which are palpable, but it has a good prognosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Follicular carcinoma shows uniform follicles with capsular and vascular invasion and spreads hematogenously, not Orphan Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies.
explanation_incorrect.C: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and shows polygonal cells in amyloid stroma with elevated calcitonin.
explanation_incorrect.D: Anaplastic carcinoma affects older patients with rapidly enlarging neck masses, compressive symptoms, and pleomorphic cells.
explanation_incorrect.E: Follicular adenoma is a benign, noninvasive follicular lesion without the nuclear clearing, grooves, or psammoma bodies described.

educationalObjective: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, with Orphan Annie nuclei, psammoma bodies, childhood irradiation risk, and a good prognosis.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 52-year-old man has a solitary thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration yields follicular cells but cannot distinguish benign from malignant. The resected specimen shows uniform follicles with tumor extending through the capsule and into surrounding vessels. He subsequently develops lung metastases.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this tumor?

options.text: Papillary carcinoma with a RET/PTC rearrangement and psammoma bodies
Medullary carcinoma with amyloid stroma and raised calcitonin
Follicular adenoma without capsular or vascular invasion
Follicular carcinoma with capsular and vascular invasion and hematogenous spread
Anaplastic carcinoma with pleomorphic cells and rapid progression

explanation_correct: Follicular carcinoma is defined by invasion of the tumor capsule and vasculature, which is the key feature separating it from follicular adenoma. Fine-needle aspiration often cannot distinguish the two because both show uniform follicles; the diagnosis depends on histologic demonstration of invasion. Spread is characteristically hematogenous, explaining the lung metastases. It has a good prognosis and is associated with RAS mutations and PAX8-PPAR-gamma translocations.

explanation_incorrect.A: Papillary carcinoma has Orphan Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies and typically spreads through lymphatics rather than hematogenously.
explanation_incorrect.B: Medullary carcinoma derives from parafollicular C cells with sheets of polygonal cells in amyloid stroma and calcitonin production, not uniform follicles.
explanation_incorrect.C: Follicular adenoma lacks capsular and vascular invasion and would not metastasize to the lung.
explanation_incorrect.E: Anaplastic carcinoma shows marked pleomorphism and frequent mitoses in older patients with rapidly enlarging neck masses and a very poor prognosis.

educationalObjective: Follicular carcinoma requires histologic demonstration of capsular or vascular invasion, spreads hematogenously, and cannot be distinguished from follicular adenoma by FNA alone.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 40-year-old man with a family history of thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma presents with a neck mass. Serum calcitonin is markedly elevated. Resection shows sheets of polygonal cells embedded in an acellular stroma that stains with Congo red.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and its associated genetic syndrome?

options.text: Papillary carcinoma; associated with BRAF mutation and childhood irradiation
Follicular carcinoma; associated with PAX8-PPAR-gamma and RAS mutations
Anaplastic carcinoma; associated with dedifferentiation of papillary carcinoma
Follicular adenoma; not associated with any inherited syndrome
Medullary carcinoma; associated with MEN 2A and MEN 2B and RET mutations

explanation_correct: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and produces calcitonin. Histology shows sheets of polygonal cells in an amyloid stroma that stains with Congo red. It is associated with MEN 2A and MEN 2B, both caused by RET mutations, which also explains the family history of thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Papillary carcinoma is linked to RET/PTC rearrangements rather than germline RET mutations and lacks calcitonin and Congo-red–positive amyloid.
explanation_incorrect.B: Follicular carcinoma is associated with RAS and PAX8-PPAR-gamma alterations but does not produce calcitonin or amyloid.
explanation_incorrect.C: Anaplastic carcinoma is a dedifferentiated tumor of older patients, not a C-cell neoplasm with amyloid stroma.
explanation_incorrect.D: Follicular adenoma is benign and is not associated with MEN syndromes or elevated calcitonin.

educationalObjective: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a calcitonin-producing C-cell tumor with Congo-red amyloid stroma and a strong association with MEN 2A/2B and RET mutations.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 75-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging, hard neck mass over 6 weeks. He has new difficulty breathing and swallowing as well as hoarseness. Biopsy shows highly pleomorphic cells with frequent mitoses. The prognosis is extremely poor.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Papillary carcinoma
Anaplastic carcinoma
Follicular carcinoma
Medullary carcinoma
Toxic multinodular goiter

explanation_correct: Anaplastic (undifferentiated) carcinoma occurs in older patients and presents with a rapidly enlarging neck mass that causes compressive symptoms such as dyspnea, dysphagia, and hoarseness. It consists of pleomorphic cells with frequent mitoses and carries a very poor prognosis. It may arise de novo or, more often, from dedifferentiation of a preexisting follicular or papillary carcinoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Papillary carcinoma has an indolent course and good prognosis with Orphan Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies, not rapid compressive growth.
explanation_incorrect.C: Follicular carcinoma has a good prognosis, uniform follicles, and hematogenous spread rather than striking pleomorphism.
explanation_incorrect.D: Medullary carcinoma shows polygonal cells in amyloid stroma with calcitonin production and a more gradual course.
explanation_incorrect.E: Toxic multinodular goiter is a benign hyperfunctioning multinodular gland, not an invasive mass producing compressive symptoms.

educationalObjective: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is a highly aggressive tumor of older patients with pleomorphic cells, rapid compressive growth, and a very poor prognosis.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 44-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy for papillary carcinoma. On the first postoperative day she develops hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. Her serum calcium is normal. There is no neck swelling or respiratory distress.
question: Which of the following best explains this complication?

options.text: Removal of the parathyroid glands causing postoperative hypocalcemia
Injury to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve during ligation of the superior thyroid vascular pedicle
Transection of the recurrent laryngeal nerve during ligation of the inferior thyroid artery
Injury to the phrenic nerve during cervical dissection
Postoperative hemorrhage compressing the trachea

explanation_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerve lies close to the inferior thyroid artery, and ligation of that artery during thyroidectomy can transect the nerve. Injury produces dysphagia and dysphonia (hoarseness), matching this patient's presentation. In contrast, injury to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve during ligation of the superior thyroid vascular pedicle causes loss of tenor, typically noticed by professional voice users, rather than the dysphagia and hoarseness seen here.

explanation_incorrect.A: Parathyroid removal causes hypocalcemia with tetany and positive Chvostek or Trousseau signs; her calcium is normal and her deficit is voice and swallowing.
explanation_incorrect.B: Superior laryngeal nerve external branch injury causes loss of high-pitched tenor voice in professional voice users, not combined hoarseness and dysphagia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Phrenic nerve injury causes diaphragmatic paralysis with dyspnea rather than hoarseness and difficulty swallowing.
explanation_incorrect.E: Postoperative hemorrhage with tracheal compression would cause respiratory distress and neck swelling, which are absent here.

educationalObjective: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury during inferior thyroid artery ligation causes hoarseness and dysphagia, whereas superior laryngeal nerve injury causes loss of tenor.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has a 2-cm solitary thyroid nodule with no suspicious cervical lymph nodes. She is euthyroid and has no compressive symptoms. The clinician wants tissue diagnosis before deciding on the extent of any surgery.
question: Which of the following is the standard initial diagnostic procedure for evaluating this thyroid nodule?

options.text: Fine-needle aspiration of the nodule
Measurement of serum calcitonin as the first-line test
Radioiodine scanning of every thyroid nodule
Immediate total thyroidectomy without tissue diagnosis
Serum TSH measurement alone as the definitive test

explanation_correct: Thyroid cancer is typically diagnosed by fine-needle aspiration, and definitive treatment is thyroidectomy. FNA cytology can identify papillary carcinoma with its Orphan Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies and medullary carcinoma with its polygonal cells and amyloid. However, it cannot reliably distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma because capsular or vascular invasion cannot be assessed on a cytology specimen.

explanation_incorrect.B: Serum calcitonin is useful for suspected medullary carcinoma but is not the routine first-line test for an undiagnosed thyroid nodule.
explanation_incorrect.C: Radioiodine scanning can classify a nodule as hot or cold, but most cancers are cold and the scan cannot separate benign from malignant cold nodules.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thyroidectomy without a tissue diagnosis is not standard practice; FNA results guide the extent of surgery.
explanation_incorrect.E: TSH may be part of the evaluation but cannot determine whether a nodule is benign or malignant.

educationalObjective: Fine-needle aspiration is the standard initial test for a thyroid nodule, although it cannot distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma.
